lines.text: 2 Problem statement
As stated in the introduction, separation of the two
components of eye movements was carried out. Dual mode
tracking eye movements are composed of smooth pursuit
and saccades. The latter are characterised by an abrupt
change of the eye velocity. This sudden variation can be
seen as a jump in the model representing the velocity of
the eye movement signal. Thus the problem presented here
will consist in discriminating jumps representing actual
saccades. This problem can be investigated as follows.
Given a sampled recording of the eye movement {Yo,
.... Ym}, one should decide which of the two hypotheses H o
and H 1 defined below is true:
Ho:Yo ..... y, follows a model M o representing the
smooth pursuit
H 1 : there exist two instants of time 0, O' such that {Yo,
{Yo'+ 1. ... y,} follow a model M o and {Yo .... Yo'}
follows a model M 1 representing the saccadic movement.
It is assumed that the probability of having a double
saccade, leading to a H 2 hypothesis, is very low and can be
ignored in a first approach.
For this p({et}/Ho) is improved against p({~,}/Ht) where
{et} represents an indicator generated with the aid of the
model M o such that p({et}/Ho) will be maximum and
p({~,}/Hx) will be minimum; p({e,}/Hi) represents the con-
ditional probability density of {et} under H i hypothesis.
Therefore, a general scheme for saccade detection will
consist of elaboration of the model Mo, under H o hypoth-
esis and generation of the indicator and testing of the
hypothesis.

4 Detection algorithm
4.1 Hypothesis testing
The principle of this proposed method is based on a
two-hypothesis test. This implies the generation of an indi-

and PESCHON, 1971). It is defined as the difference between
the actual signal measurement and the expected value of

4.3 Localisation of the beginning and the end of a saccade
Once an abnormality is detected by a test on the inno-
vation, the problem is to estimate the two instants of time

saccadic movement, respectively. The latter acts on the

4.4 Algorithm
The principle of the method described above is sum-
marised as follows. An AR model of the smooth pursuit
velocity is identified and used to construct a Kalman filter.
Then the actual eye velocity is compared with the predic-
tion generated by the filter,
The ensuing sequence of innovations allows the detec-
tion of fast phase events. The occurrence of a saccade is
confirmed by a chi 2 test. Then, the extrema of the identi-
fied saccade (0, 0') are estimated using a Hinkley algo-
rithm. Note that the detection can be achieved using the
Hinkley test; but it is preferable to use the chi 2 test which
gives a significance level. The Hinkley algorithm is only
switched on by the chi 2 test when a saccade has been
detected. Finally, smooth pursuit and saccades are separ-
ated,

Two spots of light with different shapes were presented on

band Gaussian white noise generator, the maximum excur-
sion of which was limited to a range of __+ 10 cm, with zero

Eye movement was recorded using an optoelectronic
device derived from an original design by BACH et al.
(1983). In brief, a two-dimensional photosensitive detector
provided continuous position change of a light spot reflec-
ted by the scleral surface while the eye rotated. A set of
lenses was used to focus the image reflected by the eye on
the photosensor surface. The light source was provided by
three miniature infra-red emitting diodes.
The elements of this eye monitoring device were
arranged in a tube mounted on an adjustable aluminium
frame which was supported on a very lightweight helmet.
The tube was placed in a vertical position in front of the
eye and perpendicular to the direction of sight.
The infra-red beams of light going to the eye and reflec-
ted by the eye were transmitted by an infra-red mirror
attached to the bottom of the tube and inclined at an angle
of 45 ~ with respect to the vertical. Hand position was
detected using a potentiometric device. Target, eye and

hand position signals were sampled at a frequency of
1000Hz and were low-pass filtered at 300Hz for anti-
aliasing purposes. A bandwith of 300 Hz was chosen so as
not to filter out the saccades (BAmLL et el., 1981). As a

6 Results
An illustration of the experimental results obtained is
presented in Fig. 6. The typical recording of eye tracking
movements of a random moving target (top trace) shows
the smooth and saccadic movement pattern. After identifi-
cation of smooth pursuit and saccades, the smooth com-
ponent was constructed by concatenation of the successive
segments, and respective positional offset corresponding to
the saccade amplitude was added. Smoothing of the signal
was obtained by digital filtering (2Hz) and cubic inter-
polation. The saccadic component was constructed by
chronological juxtaposition of the saccades. The integrated
sequence of innovations shows saccade detection. Separa-
tion of the two components allows quantification of their
respective contribution to eye movements. Gain and phase
of the smooth pursuit as a function of frequency were
analysed further to evaluate the alteration of oculo-manual
co-ordination during hand vibration.
The error of the method verified experimentally was
related to the measurement noise. Indeed, distinction
between small saccades and signal noise was limited by the
resolution of the eye monitoring device, which was 15' of
arc. To obtain the lowest detection threshold false detec-
tions, caused by artefacts or abrupt noise variation, were
eliminated automatically according to amplitude and
duration criteria. Blinks were discarded using the same
criteria. Thus, on several recordings containing around 500
saccades, the failure rate for false identification was less
than 1 per cent.
7 Conclusion
Separation of smooth pursuit and saccadic movements
has been achieved using a two-stage process. First, an AR
model of the first derivative of the smooth component was
identified and used to determine a Kalman filter; secondly,
the innovations generated by this filter allowed saccade
detection. The localisation of the saccades was made using
a Hinkley algorithm. The probability of saccade detection
was evaluated by a statistical analysis. The experimental
results confirm the efficiency of this proposed method.
Previous algorithms for saccadic eye movement detec-
tion have generally been based on velocity threshold set-
tings (BALOH et el., 1980; BARNES, 1982) or on successive
derivatives of the signal (MATsUOKA and HARATO, 1983).
Although the velocity was used, our algorithm takes into
account both temporal characteristics (AR model) and sta-
tistical characteristics (Kalman filter) of the signal. The
main advantages of the present method are as follows.
First, within a relatively large margin of reliability, detec-
tion of saccades does not require an a priori knowledge of
their dynamics or of the eye position signal waveform.
Secondly, the method exhibits high immunity to noise and
can be applied to a broadband signal (0-300Hz), which
cannot be the case when successive derivatives are used.
Thirdly, the method is easy to use for online analysis on a
microcomputer as the Kalman filter is synthesised by a
simple recursive algorithm and only one variable

(innovation) is tested for saccade detection.
However, once the model is estimated, three parameters
have to be chosen:
(i) the size of the sliding window which is related to the
degree of freedom of the chi square test (N samples)
(ii) the detection threshold to be set according to the
'noise level' of the innovations (this threshold, associ-
ated to a probability level, quantifies the significance
of the detection).
(iii) the variances of the state and measurement noises (r,
q) known a priori, are determined empirically by suc-
cessive trials.
It is worth noting that parameter setting is rapidly
achieved with some experience. The only limitation of the
present algorithm is the use of a model which depends on
the characteristics of the tracking signal and the noise gen-
erated by the eye monitoring device. One may, however,
imagine an adaptive procedure for the estimation of these
parameters when they are time-varying.
Automatic eye movement analysis is the aim of numer-
ous investigators interested in the control of eye move-
ments. Despite the large number of algorithms proposed in
the literature, very few have been designed for general
purpose investigation. We think that with minor adapta-
tions the principle of our method can be applied to other
detection problems and more particularly to nystagmus
analysis, which is important for clinical applications.
